summary: Catalogs middleboxes, meaning devices between hosts that do more than normal IP routing, such as NATs and firewalls. It cites related IETF work and identifies issues they raise. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some boxes sit between computers and do extra things to the traffic. This sorts them into kinds and lists the problems they cause.

questions: how do middleboxes break the end to end principle
subtitle: A catalogue of the devices that sit between two hosts and do more than forward packets, and what they cost the Internet.

tldr.problem: More and more boxes on the network path do things other than normal IP routing, which strains the end-to-end principle and the hourglass model of the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a middlebox, sorts 22 kinds of them using eight facets such as protocol layer and hard versus soft state, lists related IETF work, and draws preliminary conclusions.
tldr.outcome: It finds that most middleboxes are application-layer, implicit, in-line and hard-state, and that application protocols should be designed with them in mind. It does not claim to be definitive.

today: RFC 3234 is an Informational memo from February 2002 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a snapshot of the IETF discussion at that time and explicitly makes no claim to be definitive.

sections.title: What a Middlebox Is
sections.content:
A middlebox is any intermediary device that performs functions other than the normal, standard functions of an IP router on the datagram path between a source host and a destination host. The term was coined by Lixia Zhang. A middlebox can be virtual, an embedded function of some other box, and it is never the ultimate end-system of an application session. Normal IP routing and anything below the IP layer are excluded.

The classical Internet architecture is the hourglass model: all upper layers ride over a single IP protocol, which rides over many kinds of hardware. The end-to-end principle says some functions, such as security and reliability, can only be done completely and correctly with the help of the end points. Middlebox functions dilute the role of IP as the single necessary feature and spread function throughout the network.

The RFC lists four concerns: old protocols may fail in the presence of middleboxes, there are new failure modes, configuration is no longer limited to the two ends, and diagnosis is harder.
sections.eli5: The Internet was meant to be a plain road with smart drivers at each end. Middleboxes are toll booths and detours in the middle that nobody told the drivers about.

sections.title: Eight Facets for Classifying Middleboxes
sections.content:
There is no obvious hierarchy for middleboxes, so the RFC describes eight facets for a multidimensional taxonomy. It admits the classifications are to some extent subjective and not mathematically complete. It deliberately leaves out any "good" versus "evil" scale, because middleboxes were invented for compelling reasons.

  • Protocol layer: IP, transport, upper layers, or a mix.
  • Explicit or implicit: designed into the protocol, like an SMTP relay, or an add-on like a NAT.
  • Single hop or multi-hop.
  • In-line or call-out to an ancillary box.
  • Functional or optimising: required for the session, or only an optimisation.
  • Routing or processing: choosing a direction, or changing packets or causing side effects.
  • Soft or hard state: whether a session carries on, degraded, after state is lost.
  • Failover or restart: whether a failed hard-state box is replaced with its state, or the session must restart.
sections.eli5: To compare the helpers, the memo asks the same eight questions about each one, like what it touches, whether you can see it, and what happens if it breaks.

sections.title: The Catalogue
sections.content:
Each entry ends with a brace of facet values. The 22 types include: NAT, which translates addresses on the fly and in practice always needs an application level gateway (ALG); NAT-PT, which translates between IPv6 and IPv4; the SOCKS gateway; IP tunnel endpoints; packet classifiers, markers and schedulers; transport relays; TCP performance enhancing proxies; and two kinds of load balancer, one diverting packets and one rewriting URLs.

The list continues with IP firewalls, application firewalls, ALGs, gatekeepers, transcoders, proxies, caches, modified DNS servers, content distribution boxes, application-level interceptors, application-level multicast, involuntary packet redirection and anonymisers.

A few examples of the problems noted. Terminating one TCP connection and starting another mid-path means the TCP checksum no longer covers the data end-to-end. Tunnels reduce the MTU and ICMP replies may lack diagnostic information. Some Web proxies are interception devices wrongly described as "transparent"; the RFC says interception devices are anything but transparent.

Some candidates were left out: bridges and switches that snoop ARP and IGMP, wiretaps, Mobile IP home agents, and relays in interplanetary networks.
sections.eli5: The memo walks through 22 kinds of helper boxes, from ones that swap addresses to ones that keep copies of web pages, and says what each one does and how it can go wrong.

sections.title: What the Tally Shows
sections.content:
Tabulating the rough classifications of the 22 classes, the RFC counts that 17 are application or multi-layer, 16 are implicit, 17 are multi-hop, 21 are in-line, 18 are functional, 16 have hard state and 21 must restart the session on failure. Routing and processing are evenly split.

From this it deduces that current middleboxes are mostly application-layer devices not designed as part of the relevant protocol, performing required functions, keeping hard state and aborting user sessions when they crash. It calls this a profound challenge to the end-to-end hourglass model.

It also sorts middleboxes into three broad purposes: connecting dissimilar networks, separating similar networks into zones (especially security zones), and enhancing performance. Section 3 then lists ongoing IETF work, including MIDCOM, WEBI, OPES, CDI and RSERPOOL.
sections.eli5: When the helpers are counted up, most of them work high up on the message itself, were not planned by the original rules, and make the whole trip fail if they break.

sections.title: Preliminary Conclusions
sections.content:
On the end-to-end principle, the RFC concludes that middleboxes hurt it at the packet level but do not nullify it as a desirable principle of application protocol design. Future application protocols should be designed in recognition of the likely presence of network address translation, packet diversion and packet level firewalls.

On failure, middlebox design should include a clear mechanism for dealing with failure. It describes three approaches: soft state, rapid failover to a hot spare, and rapid restart by the two ends. When middlebox functions sit at different layers, recovery cannot assume help from other layers. New application protocol designs should include explicit mechanisms for inserting middleboxes and consider the eight facets.

It also suggests common features that would be desirable: discovery and monitoring, configuration and control, call-out, routing preferences, failover and restart handling, and security including mutual authentication.
sections.eli5: The advice is to build programs that expect helpers in the middle, and to make those helpers handle their own breakage gracefully.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security risks are specific to each type of middlebox, so little can be said in general. Extra boxes in the path create extra points of attack, reduce or eliminate end-to-end encryption, and complicate trust and key distribution models.

The RFC makes three general points: interference with end-to-end transmission is a crippling impediment to generalised use of IPSEC in its present form and invalidates transport layer security in many scenarios; middleboxes require a move from two-way to N-way trust relationships and key sharing; and their management and configuration mechanisms are a tempting point of attack. Caches and content distribution also raise access control questions for content subject to copyright.
sections.eli5: Every extra helper in the middle is one more place a bad guy can try to break in, and it makes private messages harder to keep private from end to end.

items.title: Protocol layer
items.text: IP, transport, upper layers or a mix.

items.title: Explicit vs implicit
items.text: Designed into the protocol, or an add-on.

items.title: Single vs multi-hop
items.text: One box in the path, or several.

items.title: In-line vs call-out
items.text: On the data path, or via an ancillary box.

items.title: Functional vs optimising
items.text: Required for the session, or only a speed-up.

items.title: Routing vs processing
items.text: Chooses a direction, or changes packets.

items.title: Soft vs hard state
items.text: Session degrades, or fails, when state is lost.
